cards.headline: Martin County High School evacuated after bomb threat; sweep finds no evidence
cards.teaser: Martin County High School was evacuated Thursday afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, and a sweep by the Martin County Sheriff's Office found no evidence of a thre
cards.body:
Martin County High School was evacuated Thursday afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, and a sweep by the Martin County Sheriff's Office found no evidence of a threat. Students and staff returned to their classrooms and regular dismissal continued as scheduled.

 School administrators notified families of an increased law enforcement presence on campus as authorities responded to the threat. The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a comprehensive search of the school property while students and staff remained evacuated away from campus buildings.

 In an update issued at 2:55 p.m., school officials said the Martin County Sheriff's Office was finalizing its sweep of the campus and found no evidence of a threat. Students and staff were cleared to return to their classrooms, and regular dismissal procedures were expected to continue as scheduled. School officials also said bus transportation was anticipated to operate without delays.

 "Please know that students and staff remain safe," the school said in its notification to families. "Thank you for your patience and cooperation as we worked with law enforcement to ensure the safety of our students and staff." Parents were notified of the situation through a message from the school Thursday afternoon. Authorities have not released additional details about the source of the email threat.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police investigate death of unidentified man found near Okeechobee Road business
cards.teaser: Officers are working to identify a man found dead in the grass near a business on Okeechobee Road Wednesday morning. A witness told investigators the man was seen in the same spot the night before.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are investigating the death of an unidentified man found lying in the grass near a business on Okeechobee Road Wednesday morning.

 Officers responded to the 7000 block of Okeechobee Road shortly before 7 a.m. after receiving reports of an unresponsive man lying in the grass near a business. St. Lucie County Fire Rescue also responded to the incident and the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

 A witness told investigators they had seen the man lying in the same area the night before but believed he was sleeping. Detectives said they found no obvious signs of foul play. The Medical Examiner's Office will determine the cause and manner of death. Detectives are working to identify the man and the investigation remains active.

cards.headline: Florida judge recommends discipline for Boca Raton nurse over TikTok post
cards.teaser: A Florida administrative law judge has recommended disciplinary action against a registered nurse who posted a TikTok video wishing a severe birth injury on White House Press Secre
cards.body:
A Florida administrative law judge has recommended disciplinary action against a registered nurse who posted a TikTok video wishing a severe birth injury on White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt while she was pregnant. Judge Robert S. Cohen issued the recommended order Sept. 1, proposing a reprimand, $250 fine, and social media training for Alexis Backer Lawler, a labor and delivery nurse at Baptist Health Boca Raton Regional Hospital. The case now goes to the Board of Nursing for a final ruling.

 The Florida Department of Health filed an administrative complaint against Lawler on Feb. 20 after she posted the video on Jan. 22. In the video, Lawler identified herself as a labor and delivery nurse and directed graphic, profane language at Leavitt, wishing her a fourth-degree tear. The injury was described at hearing as the most severe that can occur during childbirth, requiring surgery under anesthesia and potentially additional procedures. "As a labor and delivery nurse, it gives me great joy to wish Karoline Leavitt a fourth-degree tear," Lawler said in the video.

 A final hearing was held July 14 in Tallahassee. The case centered on whether Lawler's TikTok post constituted unprofessional conduct under Florida Administrative Code Rule 64B9-8.005(14), which prohibits nurses from using abusive, threatening or foul language in front of a patient or directing such language toward a patient. Lawler argued the video was protected political speech made on her personal time, away from her workplace, and not directed at any patient.

 Cohen rejected that argument after two Baptist Health labor and delivery patients testified that they had seen the video before or around the time of their own deliveries at the hospital. Patient E.G. testified that she had been assigned Lawler as her nurse during her Jan. 5–6 delivery and later saw the video shared by her husband. She described her reaction as shock and disgust.

 "It was just inappropriate, specifically coming from someone whose job is to take care of you at one of your most vulnerable moments," E.G. testified. Another patient testified that she saw the video a few days before her own admission to Baptist Health on Jan. 24 and overheard nurses at the hospital discussing it during her stay. She said she did not have Lawler as her nurse and that her decision to deliver at Baptist Health was not changed by having seen the video. Neither patient filed or planned to file a lawsuit against the hospital or Lawler.

 Cohen found that Lawler had not taken steps to restrict her TikTok audience before posting the video and did not appear to have a clear understanding of which of her accounts were public or private. "By posting the video on TikTok, with some clearly provocative language aimed at a pregnant mom who happens to be a public figure, on a popular public social media platform, she should have known there was a risk of the posting going viral," Cohen wrote. He also noted that Lawler had identified herself as a labor and delivery nurse in the video, which he said lent specific weight to the nature of the injury she was wishing on Leavitt.

 Shortly after the video circulated, Lawler was fired from Baptist Health Boca Raton Regional Hospital. A hospital spokesperson confirmed her termination, stating that the comments made in the social media video do not reflect the hospital's values or the standards expected of healthcare professionals. Lawler's TikTok account was public at the time of the posting, and a group called Libs of TikTok reposted the video along with Lawler's place of employment, causing it to spread widely.

 Lawler testified that she subsequently received death threats and tightened her social media privacy settings. Her TikTok account has since been banned.

 The recommended order also references a separate incident from September 2025, in which Baptist Health received complaints from employees and members of the public about social media posts Lawler made related to the death of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk. Human resources records show Lawler met with hospital management, reviewed the hospital's social media policy and acknowledged the guidance.

 No formal discipline was issued at that time. Lawler was also noted to have worn a pin reading "no uterus, no opinion" while working in the labor and delivery unit. One patient testified that she found the pin off-putting in that setting.

 In weighing the penalty, Cohen cited several mitigating factors: Lawler has been licensed for approximately 14 years with no prior disciplinary history, the two patients who testified suffered no physical harm and pursued no legal action, and Lawler lost her job at Baptist Health as a result of the incident. "The mitigating factors in this case outweigh any potential aggravating factors which were not proven to exist," Cohen wrote.

 Cohen also recommended the board assess costs related to the investigation and prosecution of the case. The Board of Nursing is not required to follow the judge's recommendation.

cards.headline: Vero Beach gym owner helps Team USA win gold in paintball at France event
cards.teaser: Paige Vasser, owner of Legacy Boxing Gym in Vero Beach, helped Team USA win gold last weekend at an international paintball competition in France, capping a rapid rise that has pla
cards.body:
Paige Vasser, owner of Legacy Boxing Gym in Vero Beach, helped Team USA win gold last weekend at an international paintball competition in France, capping a rapid rise that has placed her among the top-10 professional women in the sport.

 Vasser grew up in Southeast Georgia near Brunswick before moving to Sebastian, where she eventually opened Legacy Boxing Gym in Vero Beach. She never played a sport until she was 21 years old. Her introduction to athletics came through boxing, which she embraced fully despite having never exercised before.

 Vasser said she thought boxing was, in her words, badass. Her boyfriend, who had been playing paintball for about 10 years, later introduced her to the sport. She took her team at Legacy for a day of paintballing and quickly fell in love with it as a weekend activity that kept them busy.

 What started as a weekend hobby quickly turned into something much bigger. A coach noticed Vasser playing and recruited her for his divisional team. A year later, she signed with her first women's professional team.

 Her rise through the sport has been rapid, placing her among the top professional women in paintball. Last weekend she competed internationally when she flew into Paris for an event in France.

 The event was held at the site of the United Paintball Federation, where Vasser and Team USA won gold in one of the largest competitions in the sport. Vasser said she got to play with girls she never played with before, calling it an awesome experience. She said the other players were amazing and it was a lot of fun.

 The gym owner's journey from someone who never played sports or exercised before age 21 to becoming an international gold medalist in paintball highlights her rapid development in the sport. Her story demonstrates how a weekend pastime can evolve into professional athletic success when combined with dedication and natural talent.

The injury was described at hearing as the most severe that can occur during childbirth, requiring surgery under anesthesia and potentially additional procedures. "As a labor and delivery nurse, it gives me great joy to wish Karoline Leavitt a fourth-degree tear," Lawler said in the video.

 A final hearing was held July 14 in Tallahassee. The case centered on whether Lawler's TikTok post constituted unprofessional conduct under Florida Administrative Code Rule 64B9-8.005(14), which prohibits nurses from using abusive, threatening or foul language in front of a patient or directing such language toward a patient. Lawler argued the video was protected political speech made on her personal time, away from her workplace, and not directed at any patient.

 Cohen rejected that argument after two Baptist Health labor and delivery patients testified that they had seen the video before or around the time of their own deliveries at the hospital. Patient E.G. testified that she had been assigned Lawler as her nurse during her Jan. 5–6 delivery and later saw the video shared by her husband. She described her reaction as shock and disgust.

 "It was just inappropriate, specifically coming from someone whose job is to take care of you at one of your most vulnerable moments," E.G. testified. Another patient testified that she saw the video a few days before her own admission to Baptist Health on Jan. 24 and overheard nurses at the hospital discussing it during her stay. She said she did not have Lawler as her nurse and that her decision to deliver at Baptist Health was not changed by having seen the video. Neither patient filed or planned to file a lawsuit against the hospital or Lawler.

 Cohen found that Lawler had not taken steps to restrict her TikTok audience before posting the video and did not appear to have a clear understanding of which of her accounts were public or private. "By posting the video on TikTok, with some clearly provocative language aimed at a pregnant mom who happens to be a public figure, on a popular public social media platform, she should have known there was a risk of the posting going viral," Cohen wrote. He also noted that Lawler had identified herself as a labor and delivery nurse in the video, which he said lent specific weight to the nature of the injury she was wishing on Leavitt.

 Shortly after the video circulated, Lawler was fired from Baptist Health Boca Raton Regional Hospital. A hospital spokesperson confirmed her termination, stating that the comments made in the social media video do not reflect the hospital's values or the standards expected of healthcare professionals. Lawler's TikTok account was public at the time of the posting, and a group called Libs of TikTok reposted the video along with Lawler's place of employment, causing it to spread widely.

 Lawler testified that she subsequently received death threats and tightened her social media privacy settings. Her TikTok account has since been banned.

 The recommended order also references a separate incident from September 2025, in which Baptist Health received complaints from employees and members of the public about social media posts Lawler made related to the death of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk. Human resources records show Lawler met with hospital management, reviewed the hospital's social media policy and acknowledged the guidance.

 No formal discipline was issued at that time. Lawler was also noted to have worn a pin reading "no uterus, no opinion" while working in the labor and delivery unit. One patient testified that she found the pin off-putting in that setting.

 In weighing the penalty, Cohen cited several mitigating factors: Lawler has been licensed for approximately 14 years with no prior disciplinary history, the two patients who testified suffered no physical harm and pursued no legal action, and Lawler lost her job at Baptist Health as a result of the incident. "The mitigating factors in this case outweigh any potential aggravating factors which were not proven to exist," Cohen wrote.

 Cohen also recommended the board assess costs related to the investigation and prosecution of the case. The Board of Nursing is not required to follow the judge's recommendation.

hero.headline: Martin County High School evacuated after bomb threat; sweep finds no evidence
hero.teaser: Martin County High School was evacuated Thursday afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, and a sweep by the Martin County Sheriff's Office found no evidence of a thre
hero.body:
Martin County High School was evacuated Thursday afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, and a sweep by the Martin County Sheriff's Office found no evidence of a threat. Students and staff returned to their classrooms and regular dismissal continued as scheduled.

 School administrators notified families of an increased law enforcement presence on campus as authorities responded to the threat. The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a comprehensive search of the school property while students and staff remained evacuated away from campus buildings.

 In an update issued at 2:55 p.m., school officials said the Martin County Sheriff's Office was finalizing its sweep of the campus and found no evidence of a threat. Students and staff were cleared to return to their classrooms, and regular dismissal procedures were expected to continue as scheduled. School officials also said bus transportation was anticipated to operate without delays.

 "Please know that students and staff remain safe," the school said in its notification to families. "Thank you for your patience and cooperation as we worked with law enforcement to ensure the safety of our students and staff." Parents were notified of the situation through a message from the school Thursday afternoon. Authorities have not released additional details about the source of the email threat.
